title: Chapter 170 – A Hall in Mourning
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Bell]

Twenty-two thousand and eleven.

It is the number that Nurse writes at the foot of the page, when the last line is done, and Bell reads it over her shoulder and has to put a hand on the lectern. The ink is still wet. The cracked blue ledger lies open under the lamp, and the pages beside it have been turned back, one by one, until the whole of the long morning is laid out in columns: bed number, hour, and a single word.

Rested. Rested. Rested.

It took nine hours to write. Nurse did not stop. She sat on a stool at the lectern with her small round back bent and her brown stub of ink going steadily, and when her hand cramped she shook it out and went on. Bell brought her tea at the third hour and found it cold at the sixth. Yue brought her bread and she did not eat it. At noon Cheng Hui sat down beside her without a word and began, quietly, to read out the bed numbers from the dim terrace rail, a hundred at a time, so that she could write without leaving her seat.

Now it is done. The old woman sets down the pen. She looks at the figures for a long time.

"I will have to carry the book to the ninth terrace," she says. "And read it to them."

"Read it to whom?" Bell asks.

"The dead." Nurse closes the cover gently. "It is the custom. In the Hall, when a terrace is rested, the keeper reads the names aloud to the empty beds. I did it for the first thirty-one. I did it for the forty-one. I have not yet had to do it for so many."

"There are twenty-two thousand."

"I know." Her round face is calm. "It will take until the morning."

Bell takes a long breath. She looks at the lectern, and the old woman, and the shut blue book.

"Then I will read the second half," she says.

* * *

Bell has a habit that she has told no one about.

On the evening rounds, when the chalk crosses are marked and the pulses counted, she stops at a bed on the eighth terrace that has no cross at all. Eighty-eight thousand four hundred and twelve. A woman of about sixty, thin and brown, with hazel eyes closed and her hands folded on her breast. A brass plate at the foot of the cot says only, in Nurse's careful hand, Midwife. Nothing else is known of her. Bell has sat on the stool beside the bed for three evenings now, for a quarter of an hour at a time, and read aloud from the lists of the day.

She does not know why. She tells herself it is because the woman's pulse is steady, and she likes a steady pulse. She tells herself it is because she has no patients left in the world who are not dying. But on the third evening she found herself telling the sleeper about Ao and the rabbit, and about Tao's top, and about the boy who had been eight and sat at a table, and her voice had cracked.

"You would have known what to do with them," she said, to the quiet. "You would have caught them. All of them."

The sleeper breathed. In. Out. Eleven to the minute.

Bell had patted the thin brown hand, and risen, and gone on to the next bed.

* * *

They go down to the ninth terrace at dusk, all of them.

It is a strange procession. Nurse leads, with the ledger held against her chest and the snuffer at her belt. Bell follows, with her satchel on her hip and Yue's hand in hers. Behind them come the children in a ragged line, Ao and Tao holding hands, Mo Yan with her charcoal tucked behind her ear, Duan Ke with his hand on the pale hilt, Cheng Hui with his leather book, Hai Ren with his long hands folded. Last of all, small and pale in the gloom, walks Zhen Li, with the brass lantern clenched in both fists.

The ninth terrace is dark.

It is darker than anything Bell has seen in the Hall. The blue glow that has lit the beds for six hundred years is gone, and in its place is a thick cold dimness, and the long curved rows of cots stretch away into it like the ribs of a drowned ship. The air is still. The air smells of nothing. There is no breath in it at all.

She stops at the head of the first row. Her throat has closed.

The sleepers lie as they lay. Their faces are smooth. Their hands are folded. There is no mark on them, no sign of struggle or fear. They look as they always looked, a river of the quiet dead in the faint gleam of Zhen Li's lantern, and the only difference is that nothing is rising and falling.

"Read," says Nurse.

She opens the book, and begins.

* * *

It is a sound that Bell will carry for the rest of her life.

Nurse's voice is low, even, and quite without emotion. She reads the bed number, and the name if there is a name, and the word. Bed eighty-eight thousand one. A tailor. Rested. Bed eighty-eight thousand two. Unknown. Rested. On and on, down the row, her small voice carried through the dark, and as she reads she walks, one slow step to each, and the children walk behind her.

At the second hour, Bell takes the book.

Her hands are shaking. She finds the place where Nurse's finger rests, and reads. Bed eighty-nine thousand four hundred and twelve. A weaver. Rested. She stops. She cannot go on.

She stands in the dark with the ledger open in her hands, and she looks at the bed, and the woman in it. A thin brown woman of fifty, with gray in her hair and the faint scars of a long life on her wrists. A weaver. She has seen her before. She has stopped at this bed, on three separate rounds, to count the pulse. She did not know the woman's name. She still does not.

But she knows the hands. They are the hands of a woman who has spent her life drawing thread through a loom, and who once, in some city that no longer exists, held up a finished bolt of cloth to the light and said, There. That will do.

Bell's eyes burn.

Nurse's hand comes up and rests on her wrist. "Take your time," the old woman says softly.

"I cannot—"

"Yes, you can." The grip tightens. "That is the custom. You say the name, and you say the word, and then you walk on. It is not for you. It is for them."

Bell swallows. She lifts the book.

"Bed eighty-nine thousand four hundred and twelve," she says, and her voice breaks, and mends. "A weaver. Rested."

She walks on, and does not look back, and behind her the small blue flame burns on in the dark, as steady as a heart.

* * *

At midnight, Zhen Li lights the lamp.

Bell does not see him move. She hears the small scratch of metal on stone, and turns, and sees him kneeling at the head of the terrace with the brass lantern in front of him. His face is white. His lips are moving. He has set the lantern on the floor, and is holding his two small hands cupped around it, as though it were a candle in a wind.

"Zhen Li," says Nurse, sharply.

"I'm all right."

"What are you doing?"

"There are too many." His voice is flat and faint. "I can't light twenty-two thousand lamps. But I can light one."

"One what?"

"The first." He lifts his eyes, and Bell sees that they are very wide, and entirely calm. "The Lamplighters had a custom. When a hall was rested, the keeper lit a single flame in the center of the dark, a flame that would burn as long as anyone remembered the dead. Not oil. Not wick. A flame of memory. It's the oldest lamp there is." A tiny smile. "My father taught me. He said I'd never need it."

Nurse draws in a breath. "It will cost you."

"Yes."

"It will cost you very dearly."

"I know." He looks down at the lantern. "I thought I'd give the color of the door. But I don't think that's enough. It has to be something big. Something that was mine."

Bell is already moving. She crosses the floor in three strides and drops to her knees, and seizes his wrists. "No. Zhen Li. No. You have given enough."

"Bell."

"You have given your mother's name. Your father's whistle. You do not have to give—"

"I do." His voice is gentle. "It's not for them. It's for me. If I don't do it, I'll never forgive myself." He smiles, very faintly. "And I won't remember not forgiving, so it doesn't matter."

She stares at him.

"Please," says Zhen Li. "Let me."

Her grip loosens. She cannot speak. She sits back on her heels, and presses her hands to her mouth, and nods.

* * *

The flame is small.

It is no larger than the nail of her thumb, and it hangs in the air above the brass lantern like a bead of light, trembling. It is not gold. It is not orange. It is the pale clear blue of a summer sky, the color of the light in the sleeping beds before they went out. It steadies. It brightens. And then, slowly, it rises, drifting up through the cold air of the terrace to hang in the center of the vault, where it burns, still and clear, above twenty-two thousand silent beds.

Zhen Li is on his knees, swaying.

Bell catches him as he falls. His body is weightless. His eyes are open, but they are blank and bright, like a child's who has been shown a thing too large to understand. She holds him against her chest, and says his name, and he looks up at her, puzzled.

"Hello," he says politely.

"Hello."

"Do I know you?"

"Yes." Her throat is tight. "I'm Bell. We're friends."

"Oh." He considers this. "That's nice. I like having friends." He looks round the terrace, at the dark, at the little blue flame, at the faces of the children. His gaze rests on Ao, who has crept forward with the rabbit in his arms and tears streaming down his face. "What's your name?"

Ao hiccups. He wipes his nose on the rabbit's ear, which is already damp from a great deal of earlier use. "I'm Ao."

"And I'm..." The boy frowns. "I'm sorry. I've forgotten. I think I used to know."

Ao stares at him for a moment. Then, very gravely, he steps forward and takes Zhen Li's face between his two small hands.

"You're Zhen Li," he says. "You're the lamp boy. You're my friend."

Zhen Li blinks. Something crosses his small tired face, quick as a bird's shadow, and is gone.

"Zhen Li," he says slowly, trying it out. "That's a good name."

"It's yours," says Ao.

* * *

Jian sits with her afterward on the cold stair, with the staff across his knees.

They have put Zhen Li to bed. They have put them all to bed, the little ones in a heap on the first cot with the rabbit in the middle, and the older ones on the floor. Only the two of them are awake, in the long dim corridor, with the faint sound of the shed ringing somewhere below.

"I want to say something," Jian says.

"Then say it."

"I did not feed her." His voice is low. "I promised, and I kept it. But I want you to know that I wanted to. I stood at the rail of the eighth terrace for an hour tonight, with the panel open, and my hand was ready. I had only to say the word."

Bell does not look at him. "Why didn't you?"

"Because of you." He draws a breath. "Because you stood in front of me and told me what I would be doing. And because the boy told me I should listen."

"Hm."

"I do not think I have ever been so angry at myself." His laugh is dry. "A hundred and nineteen years of being the kind of man who does the thing. And tonight I did nothing at all. I stood and watched twenty-two thousand people go dark, and I did not lift a finger."

"That is not nothing."

"It feels like it."

"It always does." She turns her head at last, and her eyes are red-rimmed. "That is what it is to be a healer. You do not save them all. You never do. You save the ones you can, and you sit with the others. It is not a smaller thing. It is only a different one."

He looks at her.

"I did not know you thought that," he says.

"I did not know it myself until tonight." A wry, cracked smile. "Now get some sleep, you old fool, before I sedate you."

* * *

Hai Ren does what he can.

He asks Bell's leave first, which is the thing she will remember. He stands at the head of the dark ninth terrace with his long hands folded and says in his dry whisper, "Some may still be breathing. The shed is a mercy, but it is not always complete. If any are caught between, I would like to ease them."

Bell looks at him. "Will it cost you?"

"It will."

"How much?"

"I do not know." He inclines his head. "But I would rather know that it was asked."

She thinks of the forty-one. She thinks of the long white face, the fall, the pulse that skipped. She thinks of how little she has said about it.

"Go," she says. "Come back when you are done. And if you fall, I will carry you."

"Thank you."

He walks away down the dim aisle, a tall thin shape in gray, and she watches until he is lost to sight. Three hours later he returns on Duan Ke's arm, white as paper, shaking, with blood on his lip. He sits down on the stone floor and says, very softly, "There were nine."

"Nine?"

"Still breathing. They are rested now." His eyes close. "I should like to sleep, if that is permitted."

Bell kneels, and takes his wrist, and counts.

* * *

Tao asks Cheng Hui whether the blue flame will go out.

He puts the question on the stair, with his face turned up and his top clutched to his chest. The scholar, who is sitting with his leather book on his knee, looks down at him and takes his time.

"I do not know," he says. "I am not a Lamplighter."

"Zhen Li said it would burn as long as anyone remembered."

"Yes."

"Then I'll remember." Tao scowls. "I'll remember it forever."

"That is an admirable resolve."

"And Ao will. And Mo Yan."

"I expect so."

Tao thinks. "What if we forget? Like Zhen Li forgot?"

Cheng Hui closes the book. For a time he is silent, and the lamplight casts a long shadow behind him up the curved wall. Then he says, very gently, "That is why we write things down, little one."

"I can't write."

"You can learn." He holds out the leather book. "Here. The first character is simple. A bar, a hook, a dot. It means flame."

Tao takes the charcoal. His small tongue pokes out. The bar is crooked, the hook is a loop, and the dot is a smudge, but when he holds it up to the light, Cheng Hui looks at it with a gravity that the boy has never seen on him.

"Excellent," says the scholar. "You have just made your first record."

Tao beams. He folds the paper, with great ceremony, and tucks it into his shirt.

* * *

Mei speaks to Bell in the small hours, through the grille, when the others have gone to rest.

It is a very thin voice now, barely more than a breath, and Bell has to put her ear to the cold metal to catch it. Is it over? the girl says.

"Not yet. Nurse thinks the Hall will keep going until you are back above the line. We do not know how long that will take."

I'm so sorry.

"It is not your fault."

It is a little bit my fault. A tiny, honest laugh. I said yes to the memory. I knew it would cost something. I didn't know it would cost so many.

Bell closes her eyes. She leans her forehead against the grille. "Mei," she says. "May I tell you something?"

Yes.

"I have delivered nine hundred and six infants. I have lost four. I remember every one of them." Her voice is steady. "And I will tell you what I tell every mother who loses a child. It was not the thing you did. It was the thing that happened. You are a part of it. You are not the cause."

A long silence. Then, so quietly that she nearly misses it: Thank you.

"You are eleven years old," says Bell. "You are not responsible for the end of the world."

I know. A small sniff. But I'd like to be responsible for the beginning of the next one.

Bell laughs, helplessly, and wipes her eyes with the back of her hand.

"You will be," she says. "I have seen you. You will be a very good one."

Will you tell Papa?

"Tell him what?"

That I said so. The thread of a voice wavers. He worries. He thinks I am only sad. I want him to know that I am a little bit brave, too.

"I will tell him in the morning."

Thank you, Bell.

Bell stays at the grille until the voice has gone quiet, and the small steady breath of the sleeping girl has replaced it. Then she folds her cloak round her shoulders, and goes out into the dark corridor to find her bed.

* * *

The shed does not stop.

Bell hears it at dawn, from the corridor. It is the low, rising note again, the single tone from the walls, climbing and holding and falling. She is sitting on the floor outside the Annex with her back to the wall and Zhen Li asleep across her knees, and she lifts her head and listens, and a cold hand closes round her heart.

Yue comes running down the passage with her slate in her fist. She does not write. She only holds it up, blank, and points at her feet, and mouths, Eight.

"Eight?"

The eighth terrace. Yue's face is gray. It's starting. I can feel it in the floor.

Bell is on her feet. She lays Zhen Li gently on the bench, and tucks the blanket round him, and runs.

The eighth terrace is above the ninth. She reaches it at a dead run, up the spiral, past the dark landing and the ruined lamps, and stops at the rail with her chest heaving. It is just beginning. The rows closest to the wall have gone dim. The lights are going out in a thin line along the outer curve, and the dark is moving inward like a tide.

She has no time to think. She runs down the nearest aisle, between the rows, with her satchel banging against her hip, and stops at a bed she knows.

Eighty-eight thousand four hundred and twelve.

The midwife.

Bell kneels. She takes the thin brown wrist, and finds the pulse, and it is there. Slow. Thready. A little uneven. But there. She had thought, in the dark, in the endless reading of the names, that the woman was on the ninth terrace. She is not. She is on the eighth. She has been alive all this time.

"Oh," says Bell. "Oh, no."

She holds the wrist.

The glow along the rail flickers and dims. The woman's face, which was lit softly gold, goes gray. And Bell, who has delivered nine hundred children, and held the hands of the dying, and never once been afraid, finds that she is weeping.

* * *

She does not know how long she sits there.

She holds the hand. She counts the pulse. It slows, and slows, and slows. Behind her she hears footsteps and does not turn. A hand rests on her shoulder, and she knows from the quiet that it is Hai Ren, and from the weight that it is Jian. She does not look up.

"She is still here," she whispers. "She's still breathing."

"I know," says the monk.

"I can't let her go alone."

"No."

"She doesn't have anyone. She doesn't have a name. There's no one to read her."

"There is you," says Jian, gently.

Bell lowers her head. She puts her forehead against the cold rail. And she begins, in a low cracked voice, to talk.

She tells the woman who she is. She tells her about the valley, and the orchard, and the old house with its rag rug and its stove. She tells her about a boy who once came out of a river with a fever, and the girl who nursed him, and how, a hundred years later, she is still nursing him, and still losing the argument. She tells her about the children in the Annex, and the little one with the rabbit, and the monk who put forty-one to rest. She talks, and talks, and the pulse in her fingers falters, and steadies, and falters.

And the woman on the bed opens her eyes.

* * *

They are hazel, and clouded, and wide. They fix on Bell's face, and for a moment there is nothing in them at all.

Then the thin brown lips move, and a voice like dry paper whispers, "Is it a boy?"

Bell cannot breathe.

"Is it a boy or a girl?" the woman says. "I can't see. Tell me. Is it breathing?"

"Yes," says Bell.

She does not decide to say it. It comes from somewhere deeper than thought.

"Yes," she says again, and her voice is steady. "It's breathing. She's breathing. It's a girl."

"A girl." The cracked lips curve. "Is she... is she all right?"

"She's perfect." The tears are running down her face and she lets them. "She's got ten fingers and ten toes, and a head full of black hair. She's crying. Can you hear it? She's got a good strong cry."

"I hear it." The woman's eyes close. A long, slow breath leaves her. "Oh, I hear it."

"Hold her," says Bell. "Here. Take her."

She lays her own hand, hard and warm, over the thin brown one. The woman's fingers curl round it. They tighten. They hold on, with the faint desperate grip of a person who has just done the oldest and hardest thing in the world.

"There you are," whispers the midwife. "There you are, little one."

The fingers go slack.

Bell sits very still. The light on the rail goes out. In the dark, the Hall rings its single note, rising and holding and falling, and then, quite suddenly, it stops. There is no echo. The silence that follows is so complete that she can hear the beating of her own heart. The shed has ended. Mei, somewhere far below, has crossed the line. And under the silence she hears the footsteps of the children coming up the stair, and the quiet voice of Nurse, beginning to read.

Bed eighty-eight thousand four hundred and twelve, says Nurse. A midwife.

Bell lays down the hand.

Rested.
